title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 90
paragraphs: Now on the same day on which the defeat took place at Plataea, another, as fortune would have it, took place at Mycale in Ionia. When the Greeks who had come in ships with Leotychides the Lacedaemonian were lying at Delos, there came to them as envoys from Samos Lampon son of Thrasycles, Athenagoras son of Archestratides, and Hegesistratos son of Aristagoras — who had been sent by the people of Samos without the knowledge either of the Persians or of the tyrant Theomestor son of Androdamas, whom the Persians had set up as tyrant of Samos. When these were brought before the commanders, Hegesistratos spoke at length using all kinds of arguments, saying that as soon as the Ionians saw them, they would at once revolt from the Persians, and that the barbarians would not await the attack; and if after all they did, the Greeks would take a prize such as they would never take again thereafter. Appealing to the gods worshipped in common, he tried to persuade them to rescue men who were Greeks from slavery and to drive the barbarian away. This was easy for them to do, he said, because the enemy's ships sailed badly and were no match for theirs in battle. Moreover, if the Greeks suspected they were trying to lead them on by fraud, the envoys were ready to be taken as hostages in their ships.
